tasks.question: Why does it matter which specific filesystem-extend command you use?
options: A) It doesn't matter — resize2fs works universally on any filesystem type, including XFS

B) The correct command depends on the actual filesystem type: resize2fs is specifically for ext2/ext3/ext4 filesystems, while xfs_growfs is specifically for XFS filesystems — running the wrong one for the actual filesystem type will fail or do nothing useful
C) xfs_growfs is a universal command that works on any filesystem, making the filesystem type irrelevant
D) The filesystem type only matters for encryption settings, not for resize operations

tasks.scenario: You run 'growpart /dev/xvdf1 1' (specifying the partition device instead of the disk device) and then try to run resize2fs.
tasks.error_shown:
$ growpart /dev/xvdf1 1
FAILED: partition 1 not found in /dev/xvdf1 (device does not contain a partition table)

$ resize2fs /dev/xvdf1
resize2fs: Filesystem does not fit! (still reports the old 98GB size)
tasks.diagnosis: growpart needs to target the DISK device (xvdf, which contains the partition table) and be told WHICH partition number to grow (1), not the partition device itself (xvdf1). Running growpart against xvdf1 fails because xvdf1 is already a partition, not a disk with a partition table to modify — this is a common mix-up between the disk device and its partitions.
tasks.fix: Re-run the command correctly targeting the disk device with the partition number as a separate argument: 'growpart /dev/xvdf 1' (grow partition 1 on disk xvdf), THEN run 'resize2fs /dev/xvdf1' (the actual partition device) to extend the filesystem. The two commands take different kinds of device arguments and mixing them up is an easy, common mistake.
tasks.explanation: This real, common command-syntax gotcha — for growpart disk device + partition number is needed, for resize2fs partition device only is needed. Two commands different different argument expect does, confuse doing easy, but error message-a paathu diagnose to do can.

cases.case_1: reporting-db-01's data volume — moderate, steady database IOPS needs, no extreme performance requirements
cases.case_2: A new, latency-critical payment-processing database needing guaranteed, consistent high IOPS regardless of any other activity on the account
cases.case_3: A volume storing large log files that get written sequentially and read in big sequential batches for periodic analysis, rarely accessed randomly
cases.case_4: A volume holding old compliance backups that are almost never accessed, where cost is the primary concern

correct_answers.case_1: gp3 — balanced, cost-effective performance fits a moderate, steady database workload without paying for guarantees it doesn't need
correct_answers.case_2: io2 — guaranteed, consistent high IOPS is exactly io2's purpose, justified here by the payment system's genuine latency-criticality
correct_answers.case_3: st1 — throughput-optimized HDD is designed exactly for large sequential read/write patterns like batch log analysis, at lower cost than SSD options
correct_answers.case_4: sc1 — cold HDD, the cheapest option, fits rarely-accessed backup data where retrieval speed barely matters

tasks.scenario: karthik-dev asks whether reporting-db-01 should actually be upgraded to io2 'to be safe,' given the disk-space scare. gp3 costs roughly ₹6.80/GB-month; io2 costs roughly ₹9.50/GB-month for the storage alone, PLUS a per-IOPS charge that gp3 doesn't have at this performance level.
tasks.question: Is upgrading to io2 a reasonable response to what was actually a disk-space (capacity) problem, not a performance (IOPS) problem?
tasks.solution: No — the incident was about running out of SPACE, not about insufficient IOPS or performance. reporting-db-01's actual workload (moderate, steady reporting queries) has never shown IOPS-related bottlenecks. Switching to io2 would cost roughly ₹2.70/GB-month more in storage alone (for 250GB, about ₹675/month extra) PLUS ongoing per-IOPS charges, all to solve a problem (guaranteed IOPS) that was never actually the issue. The right response to a space problem is more space (already done) and better monitoring to resize proactively next time, not a different, more expensive volume type.
